analysis.one_liner: Delays union representation elections by requiring at least 35 days before workers can vote.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: it received no markup, no vote, and no floor action before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the rules for workplace union elections. It would require at least 14 days before a hearing on a union petition, at least 35 days before workers actually vote, and it would let elections be held up and certification delayed until every legal dispute is resolved. It would also require employers to hand over a list of eligible voters with contact info. The overall effect is to slow elections down — restoring a longer timeline like the one federal labor regulators replaced in 2014, when they shortened elections that had averaged around five weeks. Employers get more time between a petition and a vote; workers who want a union spend more weeks exposed to an anti-union campaign before they can vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers facing a union organizing drive benefit most. Under current rules an election can happen in roughly two to three weeks; this bill guarantees a minimum of 35 days, plus a 14-day wait before the pre-election hearing even begins, and lets certification of the results wait until all disputes are decided. That extra time is when employers typically run meetings and one-on-one campaigns against the union — the period union researchers call the most effective for defeating organizing drives.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a waiting period of at least 14 calendar days after a petition is filed before the NLRB can even begin its hearing on representation issues.
Requires union elections to be held no earlier than 35 calendar days after a petition is filed, instead of the compressed timeline the NLRB adopted in 2014.

Delays certification of election results until the Board has ruled on every pre-election issue and any dispute about the conduct of the election itself, which gives losing employers more chances to challenge the outcome.
Requires the employer, at least 7 days after the bargaining unit is set, to provide a list of all eligible voters with names plus one form of contact information, made available to all parties.

analysis.who_pays: Workers trying to form a union. They wait at least five weeks between filing and voting, and weeks more before the result is certified. Research on union elections consistently shows that the longer a campaign runs, the more likely employer opposition — mandatory meetings, supervisor pressure, and in many cases paid anti-union consultants — will turn workers against the union before the vote. A union that wins might also face prolonged legal challenges before certification.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers trying to organize a union

drawbacks.text: Employers argue they need adequate time to prepare for a hearing, understand the proposed bargaining unit, and communicate with employees before a vote; the bill's supporters framed it as fairness and due process for both sides.

The strongest objection is the bill's effect on election timing: guaranteeing a minimum of 35 days and a 14-day hearing wait directly lengthens the window in which employer anti-union campaigns operate, the period most associated with union election losses.

Delaying certification until all disputes are resolved means workers who vote for a union may wait months longer before bargaining actually begins, and it expands the issues that can be litigated before a result counts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For employers who oppose a union drive, the extra weeks are a real benefit. For workers, the costs are significant: a guaranteed minimum five-week campaign, slower hearings, and delayed certification, each of which makes organizing harder. There is a genuine fairness argument — both sides get the voter list, and the hearing is restructured as a non-adversarial process — but the bill's core change is the delay itself, and delay in union elections overwhelmingly favors the employer side. The bill never advanced far enough for these tradeoffs to be tested in a committee or floor debate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never scheduled a markup or vote; it died there when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 14, 2017 by Senator Lamar Alexander and read twice before being referred to the Senate HELP Committee.
Eighteen Republican senators cosponsored the bill, all joining at introduction; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored it.
No further action was ever recorded — no committee markup, no committee vote, no floor action — and the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers and unions are better off because the bill died: the NLRB's shorter election timeline stayed in place, so employees voting on a union keep faster elections and quicker certification. Employers facing organizing drives, who would have gained the guaranteed minimum 35-day campaign window, gained nothing.

industries.note: The bill guarantees at least 35 days between a union petition and an election, plus a 14-day wait before the hearing, giving employers a longer window to run anti-union campaigns before employees vote. Delaying certification until all disputes are resolved also extends the period a union victory can be held up in challenges.

industries.industry: Union-avoidance consultants and management-side labor law firms
industries.note: Longer election campaigns are the core product of the paid anti-union consulting industry; a guaranteed minimum campaign window creates more billable engagement for firms hired to defeat organizing drives. This follows from the bill's delay requirements rather than any named provision.

Slower elections and delayed certification make it harder and costlier for unions to win recognition and start bargaining, directly reducing new organizing. Unions' interest in faster elections runs with workers' interest in voting quickly.
